title: The Destruction of Black Wall Street

beats.text: On the morning of June the first, 1921, black smoke rose over the north side of Tulsa, Oklahoma.
By the afternoon, a whole Black neighborhood had burned. Homes, churches, shops, and a business district.
Its name was Greenwood. Its main street was called the Negro Wall Street. Today, we know it as Black Wall Street.
What happened there was left out of the history books for most of a century.
This is the story of how Greenwood was built, how it was destroyed, and how it was forgotten.
Chapter one. Greenwood.
In the early 1900s, oil was found near Tulsa, and the town became a boom town.

visual.caption: Shooting an oil well near Tulsa, about 1910

beats.text: Money poured in, and the city grew fast.
But Tulsa was a segregated city. Black residents were shut out of the white part of town.
So they built their own, north of the Frisco railroad tracks.
Black landowners such as O. W. Gurley and J. B. Stradford bought land there, and sold lots to other Black families.

visual.title: O. W. Gurley · J. B. Stradford

beats.text: Stradford built a modern brick hotel on Greenwood Avenue.
By 1921, about ten thousand Black people lived in Greenwood.
It had two newspapers, a public library branch, churches, and scores of businesses.

visual.title: Two newspapers
visual.sub: a library branch · churches · scores of businesses

beats.text: Grocers and barbers, tailors and cafés, doctors and lawyers. And a movie theater, the Dreamland.
Booker T. Washington is said to have called it the Negro Wall Street.

visual.by: a name attributed to Booker T. Washington

beats.text: Most of its people were working people. Many worked in white homes and businesses across the tracks, and came home to Greenwood.
But what they built there was their own.
Chapter two. The spark.
On Monday, May the thirtieth, 1921, a nineteen-year-old Black shoe shiner named Dick Rowland stepped into an elevator in the Drexel Building, downtown.
The elevator operator was a seventeen-year-old white woman named Sarah Page.
Something happened in that elevator. Most likely, he stepped on her foot, or stumbled. She cried out, and he ran.
The next morning, Rowland was arrested.
That afternoon, the Tulsa Tribune ran a story on its front page. Nab Negro for Attacking Girl In an Elevator.

visual.quote: Nab Negro for Attacking Girl In an Elevator

beats.text: Some people also remembered an editorial in the same paper, headlined To Lynch Negro Tonight.

visual.by: an editorial, as some remembered it

beats.text: No copy of it has ever been found. The page is missing from the archived copies of the paper.
Either way, word spread fast.
Chapter three. The night.
By the evening, hundreds of white people had gathered outside the courthouse, where Rowland was held.
The sheriff refused to hand him over.
In Greenwood, people feared a lynching. Around nine, about twenty-five armed Black men, many of them veterans of the First World War, went to the courthouse to offer help.
They were told they were not needed, and they went home.
Around ten, about seventy-five came back. By then, the white crowd had grown to about fifteen hundred.

stat.label: in the white crowd, against about 75

beats.text: A white man tried to take a pistol from a Black veteran. A shot went off.
Then the shooting began.
Outnumbered, the Black men fell back toward Greenwood. Fighting spread along the Frisco tracks.
The police deputized white men from the crowd.
By midnight, the first fires were burning at the edge of Greenwood.
Chapter four. The morning.
Through the night, thousands of armed white men gathered along the edge of Greenwood.
At about five in the morning, a whistle sounded.
And they crossed the tracks.
They went from house to house. They looted homes, and then they set them on fire.

visual.caption: Belongings in the street, Greenwood, 1921 (Library of Congress)

beats.text: Black Tulsans fought back, from houses and from churches. But they were badly outnumbered.
From a grain elevator, at least one machine gun fired into the district.
Airplanes circled overhead. A Black lawyer named Buck Colbert Franklin wrote what he saw.
I could see planes circling in mid-air. They grew in number and hummed, darted and dipped low.

visual.quote: I could see planes circling in mid-air. They grew in number and hummed, darted and dipped low.

beats.text: Historians still debate exactly what those planes did.
Doctor A. C. Jackson was one of the best-known surgeons in Greenwood.
When the mob came to his home, he walked out with his hands up. He was shot, and he died of his wounds.
Mount Zion Baptist Church had opened just weeks earlier. It burned.

visual.caption: A church burns in Greenwood, June 1, 1921 (Library of Congress)

beats.text: National Guard troops from Oklahoma City arrived around nine. By then, most of Greenwood was already burning.

visual.caption: Soldiers and Black Tulsans on a truck downtown, 1921 (Library of Congress)

beats.text: Black residents were rounded up and taken away under guard.

visual.caption: A truck carrying Black Tulsans, 1921 (Library of Congress)

beats.text: At 11:49 that morning, the governor declared martial law.
Chapter five. The ashes.
When it was over, the heart of Greenwood was gone.
Thirty-five city blocks had burned.
One thousand two hundred fifty-six homes were burned. Two hundred fifteen more were looted.
About ten thousand people were left homeless.
Newspapers across the country carried the story. Tulsa dead total eighty-five, said the Boston Daily Globe.
The official count was later put at thirty-six. Historians believe the real number was far higher, perhaps as many as three hundred.
Up to six thousand Black Tulsans were held under armed guard, at Convention Hall, the fairgrounds, and a baseball park.
To leave, they had to carry identification cards.

visual.caption: Entrance to the camp at the fairgrounds, 1921 (Library of Congress)

beats.text: Thousands spent the winter in tents.

visual.caption: A tent home in Greenwood, 1921 (Library of Congress)

beats.text: Residents filed claims worth more than one point eight million dollars. The claims were turned down.
The city passed a new fire ordinance that would have kept many from rebuilding.
Buck Colbert Franklin and other Black lawyers challenged it in court, working out of a tent. They won.
A grand jury blamed the violence on Black Tulsans. No white person was ever sent to prison for it.
And Dick Rowland? The charges against him were dropped.
Chapter six. The silence.
Greenwood rebuilt, house by house, with little help from the city.
But the massacre itself was left out of the history books. For decades, it was barely taught, even in Tulsa.
In 1997, Oklahoma created a commission to investigate. Its report, in 2001, recommended reparations.
In 2020, researchers began searching Oaklawn Cemetery for the graves of victims.

visual.caption: Oaklawn Cemetery, Tulsa, 2020 (Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress)

beats.text: In January 2025, the U.S. Justice Department called it a coordinated, military-style attack on Greenwood.

visual.quote: A coordinated, military-style attack on Greenwood.

beats.text: It also found that no one responsible was still alive to prosecute.
Greenwood was built by people who had been shut out, and who made something of their own.
In one night and one morning, it was burned to the ground.
Then the story was buried, for most of a century.
That was Black Wall Street. Subscribe for more.
